messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Robert, a 66-year-old software engineer, had spent most of his career writing code in quiet offices, but the silence of his home office now felt like a fragile truce. He could not remember a time when his body was not on alert. The memory that anchored his vigilance came from a winter evening when he was seven: his father’s hand closing on his shoulder, the cold draft from the open window slicing across his bare skin a moment before the belt came down. The sensation of that chill on his skin, the sudden pounding in his chest, had become a permanent recording. Even now, decades later, the feeling of a particular cool draft against his arm could make him flinch before his mind caught up, or his own heart thumping after a brisk walk could trigger a visceral flash of that small boy waiting for the next blow.

He had learned early that safety meant scanning. In any room, his eyes would automatically catalog objects that could be used as weapons—a pair of scissors on the desk, a heavy glass paperweight, a kitchen knife left by the sink. He knew it was irrational, but the scanning was automatic, a habit so ingrained it felt like part of his vision. His body often jumped before his thoughts did. If his wife touched his shoulder from behind, he would jerk away with a sharp breath, his heart already racing, his hands raised before he registered it was only her. He hated that reaction almost as much as the apologetic look that followed.

For years, Robert had managed his life by keeping people at a distance. He had a handful of old colleagues from his early days at the firm, men he used to have lunch with, but he had stopped accepting invitations decades ago. Seeing them meant small talk, and small talk meant the risk of a handshake or a clap on the back. He could not bear physical contact—not a handshake, not a pat, not even a friendly arm around the shoulder. The sensation of another person’s skin against his felt like an intrusion that reignited that cold draft. He also avoided looking at his own body in the mirror, especially his back. His father’s marks had faded, but the scars were still there, and seeing them brought the memory too close. He showered quickly, in dim light, and dressed without pausing to inspect.

His wife, Karen, had learned over the years not to startle him, though she sometimes forgot. She had also learned not to ask too many questions about why he flinched. But recently, she had noticed he was pulling away even from her. She had suggested couples therapy, then gently said he should see someone on his own. Robert agreed because he was tired. Tired of the constant scanning, tired of feeling like an outsider in his own family. At holiday gatherings with Karen’s relatives, he would stand by the wall, watching everyone laugh and embrace, certain that he did not belong. He had come to believe that people could not be trusted—not because they were malicious, but because trust required a vulnerability he could not afford. Being careful had kept him alive as a child; now it was keeping him isolated.

What finally brought him to therapy was a single incident. A few weeks ago, Karen reached out to steady him when he stumbled on the stairs, and he had shoved her back with a shout. The look on her face—hurt, afraid—stayed with him. He was terrified that he might do it again, that his body would act before his mind could catch up. He wanted to stop living like a soldier still waiting for an attack that ended sixty years ago, but he had no idea how to lower his guard. He hoped, more than anything, that someone could show him how to be in a room without first checking the exits.
